To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mass and number densities of quiescent galaxies increase by factors of 5-10 from z = 2 to the local universe, while the mass density in actively star-forming galaxies remains constant.

(1) the mass density of star forming galaxies remains constant from z = 1.2 to 0.4, while the mass density of quiescent galaxies increases by a factor >2, (2) the mass density in massive star forming galaxies (log M/M_sun > 10.7) decreases with cosmic time, while the mass in less massive star forming galaxies remains flat, and (3) the number density of massive star forming galaxies decreases by a factor of >3,
the mass density of quiescent galaxies grows rapidly from z = 2 to 0, and this growth is driven by the mass buildup of individual galaxies, which are formed from star-forming galaxies by quenching.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation of galaxies, and the evolution of galaxies, and how they are linked.
the evolution of the stellar mass function of star-forming, quiescent, and total galaxy populations at 0.2 ≤ z ≤ 1.5, and the evolution of the mass function at 0.1 ≤ z ≤ 0.2.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the bimodal distribution of galaxies at the present day is a result of a continuous buildup of both star-forming and quenched populations over cosmic time, with the quiescent population growing at a faster rate than the star-forming one.
